earlier.message:
schema lang: `fixed table` declares the class, and the compiler refuses what breaks it

Glenn: "maybe we should be explicit with `fixed` to tables in schema lang" /
"that way if we add any feature that stops it from being fixed, it is a compile
error" / "otherwise, it could be a bit of a guess whether the table is fixed or
variable, couldn't it? we don't want to surprise the user." / "and enforce only
fixed tables can use message form. this saves more work." / on the guarded
branch: "the intent of the lookback conditional is to make it variable size" /
"so that is a disqualifying thing for a fixed table. not supported. only
variable."

`fixed table X` is a DECLARATION and a plain `table X` is the VARIABLE wire
always, whatever its fields are. Six constructs are refused in a fixed table's
by-value closure, each naming the field and the fixed table it breaks: a map, an
unbounded array, a pointer, a byte buffer at its used size, a guarded (`if`)
field, and a nested plain `table`. The message form is a fixed table's, and a
message-form request naming a plain table is refused naming the table.

ir.VariableTables is now the complement of the declared flag, so every emitter
switches at once; the old least-fixed-point survives as ir.FixedClosureBreaks,
which is no longer a mode but the CHECK behind the refusal. §17.2's directory
rule now asks its own question (does the closure hold a pointer, a map or an
unbounded array?) instead of reading a mode that no longer means that.

Every table that was inferred fixed took the keyword, which holds the generated
output still. bench/corpus/FixedTable.schema keeps `fixed table` and is REFUSED
here on purpose: BenchMixed's `if has_extra` guard is in its closure, and the
corpus fix belongs to the wire branch. The other guard-disqualified tables were
left plain and are listed in the PR.

No wire change.

quotes: Cut the tolerant wire. It's too much work. It was a mistake to try to do it.
That's my mistake. It's best to consistently refuse. Too much undefined behavior per-language by trying to be tolerant.
rulings.source: the maintainer, live in session, relayed verbatim in the spec brief. Scope confirmed with him: one read only, the strict read; any damage, out-of-range value, kind mismatch, broken framing or non-finite float refuses the whole load (the brief's 'with exactly one reason name' is SUPERSEDED by refusal-verdict-only: the verdict is the contract and the reason is per-language diagnostic detail); no partial value, no repair, no clamp-and-count, no reading past damage. Kept, because it is not damage: version evolution across a lawful lineage (widening, absent fields at their defaults, unknown fields from a newer writer skipped or retained, form and lineage selection). A value outside the WRITER's range is damage and refuses; it never clamps. The same for the JSON and text readers and the fixed form. Specified in docs/SPEC-TABLES.md §4, §6.5 and §13.10 and docs/FIXED-FORM-ALGORITHM.md §4.5, §4.6 and §5.4.

quotes: This is another example of trying to be too correct. It is like a softer version of trying to do partial reads. I am actually OK if there is only a generic failure to read. I do not care about the specific reporting on a per-instance basis. So for example, split it into two things 1. the thing that must be the same across all languages "failed to read" (or whatever you call it), and then the per-language specific details about why it is failing to read. That doesn't need to conform, and it can be different across languages.

Trying to make both the "failed to read" and the specific details of why the read fails, it makes each language have to write exactly the same code and do the exact same order when parsing a file. I don't think we need to be correct here.
Solve this in the simplest possible way
rulings.source: the maintainer, live in session, relayed verbatim by the coordinator, after two cold reads of the strict-only spec showed that choosing one reason across languages (first by byte order, then by a fixed rank of names) forces every language into the same code and the same check order. The cross-language read contract is the VERDICT alone: the value (identical in every language) or refused, never a partial value. Why a read refused is per-language diagnostic detail, never compared by conformance; the spec's reason vocabulary is recommended and non-normative; each language checks in whatever order is fastest for it. Specified in docs/SPEC-TABLES.md §6.5 and §13.10.
supersedes: the fixed rank of reason names and the byte-order reason selection drafted on strict-only-spec (commits 983adaed2 and 135d038b3, never on main)

every reason-identity rule: SPEC-TABLES §6.5 'Strict error identity', 'THE TABLE IS THE WHOLE ENUM, AND EVERY PORT SPELLS THE SAME SET', the same-reason requirement of the wire fuzzer (§4.2) and of the region, builder and measure paths

rulings.source: the maintainer, live in session, relayed verbatim by the coordinator, following refusal-verdict-only. 'These' are the read counters (unknown, widened, retained, retain_lost), LoadMeasure and region sizes, and (3, 4) the fuzz harness's counter and flag comparisons and diagnostic text, field names and JSON error positions: all per-language detail, never compared. The cross-language read test is: every leg reads every corpus input; a readable input is written back out (wire, and JSON and text) and the bytes are identical across legs and equal to the canonical bytes; an unreadable input is refused by every leg. Retained unknowns saved back byte-exact carry the never-clobber guarantee. Specified in docs/SPEC-TABLES.md §4, §4.2, §6.5, §6.6 and docs/plans/strict-only.md layer 3.
